learning_objective: 🎯 Step into ancient painted caves! Discover the brilliant colors and emotional depth of India's mural painting traditions from Ajanta to the Chola temples.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Ajanta (Maharashtra) has 29 Buddhist caves. The paintings (mostly 5th century CE, Vakataka period) show Jataka tales and Buddha's life. The figures have expressive faces, half-closed eyes, and incredibly graceful postures (Tribhanga).

The most famous murals in Cave 1 at Ajanta. 'Padmapani' holds a blue lotus, looking down with deep compassion. 'Vajrapani' holds a thunderbolt. They showcase masterful shading to create a 3D effect on a flat wall.

Ellora has murals representing all three religions (Hindu, Buddhist, Jain). Bagh caves (MP) are similar to Ajanta but more secular. Badami (Karnataka) features the earliest surviving Hindu murals, painted under the Chalukya kings.

South Indian temples have rich mural traditions. The Kailasanatha temple (Pallava) and the Brihadeshwara temple at Thanjavur (Chola) have exquisite paintings. Chola paintings famously show Lord Shiva (Nataraja) and royal patrons.

Developed much later (16th-18th century). Found on palace and temple walls. They are highly vibrant, using strong primary colors, and figures are painted with heavy, theatrical makeup (similar to Kathakali dancers).

fun_activity.title: 👁️ The Compassionate Gaze
fun_activity.instructions: Search for the 'Padmapani Bodhisattva' from Ajanta Cave 1. Look at his eyes and eyebrows. The artists used a technique where the eyes look downward, creating an overwhelming sense of peace and sadness for the world. Try to sketch just the eyes!

exam_tips: 📌 Expect a detailed description question on the 'Padmapani Bodhisattva' (Cave 1, Ajanta). Mention the blue lotus, the slight tilt of the head, and the shading used to create volume.
📌 Ajanta paintings are technically 'fresco secco' (painted on dry plaster), not true wet fresco.
📌 Differentiate Ajanta (purely Buddhist) from Ellora (Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain).
quick_recap: ⭐ The colors for murals were derived completely from local natural minerals and plants (like Lapis Lazuli for blue).
⭐ Badami caves contain the earliest known Brahmanical (Hindu) paintings.
⭐ Kerala murals are distinct for their vibrant colors and heavy, stylized proportions influenced by local dance dramas.
